newsitem.title: USA: U.S. unveils steps to fight new state marijuana laws.
newsitem.headline: U.S. unveils steps to fight new state marijuana laws.

text.p: The Clinton Administration said on Monday it would sanction doctors who prescribe marijuana and other drugs made legal by new California and Arizona laws and punish federal workers who use them.
It said federal anti-drug laws overrode state laws.
"Federal law enforcement provisions remain in effect," said Barry McCaffrey, director of the Office of National Drug Control Policy. "Nothing has changed."
California and Arizona voters in November approved the use of marijuana for medicinal purposes. Arizona extended the legalisation to other drugs, including heroin and LSD.
McCaffrey told a news conference that doctors could face the revocation of their practitioner's registration and be prosecuted.
He also said federal agencies would continue their efforts to fight drug use, its import and shipment by mail.

McCaffrey said that U.S. law, affirmed by the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Department of Health and Human Services, has found that marijuna has a "high potential for abuse" and "no currently accepted medicinal use."

He said federal authorities had issued a formal advisory to the transportation industry that safety-sensitive workers who test positive in required drug-testing programmes may not use state law as a legitimate explanation for the presence of prohibited drugs.
Safety-sensitive workers, such as many in the aviation, mass transit, railroad and trucking industries, face dismissal if they test positive for prohibited drugs.
The Transportation Department advisory urged private firms to follow its example and to crack down on illegal drug use.
Attorney General Janet Reno said federal prosecutors in California and Arizona would work with local authorities to assure that federal law was enforced.
McCaffrey called marijuana a "front-end" drug that can lead to more dangerous drugs. "That is the danger."

Health and Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala said "We have a problem" because drug use among teenagers was rising, noting that surveys showed past-month use of marijuana among eighth graders rose to 11.3 percent in 1996, from 9.1 percent in 1995.
"Even more disturbing," she said, "one in five 10th graders used marijuana in the past month."
Shalala added that all available research showed marijuana was dangerous, with the potential to harm the brain, heart, lungs and immune system.

She added that the National Institutes of Health would continue to review claims about the possible benefits of smoked marijuana, but that any claims made must be backed by peer-review and be scientifically valid.
McCaffrey called the laws approved by voters in California and Arizona "stealth" and hoax" initiatives not based on fact.
He said claims made for marijuana included successes in treating problems ranging from depression to writer's cramp and the claims had no scientific support.

McCaffrey said his office would work with Congress to see if any new legislation was needed to reaffirm the national policy of federal control over drugs that have a high potential for abuse and no accepted medical use.
The sponsors of California's Proposition 215 to allow medicinal marijuana use criticised Clinton's decision as "cruel" and "indefensible," and vowed a court challenge.

"The president has been drawn into General McCaffrey's new war -- a war against those physicians who believe marijuana can alleviate the suffering of their patients. This is a politically inept attempt to sabotage Prop. 215. We feel the president is about to make a grave mistake," Bill Zimmerman, who managed the campaign for Proposition 215, said.
